request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course: 
The patient, a 28-year-old male with moderate intellectual disability, presented with a history of comorbid diagnoses including autism spectrum disorder, hypertension, hypothyroidism, and GERD. The patient had a history of excoriation disorder, schizoaffective disorder bipolar type, and displayed symptoms of anxiety, irritability, and physical aggression. The patient was initially treated with quetiapine but was later transitioned to valbenazine due to intermittent abnormal movements. The patient's treatment was further adjusted, and clozapine was prescribed due to continued psychosis.

Hospital Stay: 
Four days after starting valbenazine treatment, improvement in abnormal movements was noted. Over two months, the patient no longer displayed any abnormal jaw movements, minimal to no arm/hand/finger movements or foot tapping, and no truncal movements. Caregivers reported that these improvements resulted in less isolating, aggressive, and confrontational behavior. The patient also became more cooperative, increasing participation in activities and displaying less resistance to caregiver assistance with activities of daily living. The patient currently remains stable on valbenazine (80 mg QHS).
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment: 
The patient was initially treated with quetiapine for symptoms of intermittent abnormal movements, which was later adjusted following persistent psychosis. Valbenazine was prescribed and later escalated to 80 mg QHS. Due to continued psychosis, clozapine was also introduced and titrated over 2 weeks to 300 mg daily.

Follow-up Plan: 
The patient is currently stable on valbenazine (80 mg QHS) with no reported adverse events. No further medication changes are planned at this time, and follow-up with the patient will continue to monitor for any changes in behavior or physical movements.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The episode centres on abnormal movements (jaw, arm, hand, finger, foot tapping, truncal) that improved with valbenazine, which is the treatment for tardive dyskinesia. The patient had been on quetiapine, an antipsychotic, so the movements were most likely medication-induced tardive dyskinesia.

In ICD-10-AM, tardive dyskinesia from a drug is coded to G24.0 (drug-induced dystonia) or, more specifically, G24.8 (other dystonia). The medication-induced movement disorders sit in G25.1 (drug-induced tremor) and G25.7 (other and unspecified drug-induced movement disorders). Drug-induced tardive dyskinesia is classified in the G24 category, G24.0 drug-induced dystonia. Australian practice, though, codes tardive dyskinesia to G24.0 and adds an external-cause code, Y49.-, for the antipsychotic.

The alternative is that the principal diagnosis is schizoaffective disorder (F25), since clozapine was started for continued psychosis. The narrative, however, focuses on the abnormal movements and the valbenazine response. The treatment section describes the quetiapine as treating "intermittent abnormal movements", and the diagnosis section was withheld, which suggests the withheld diagnosis is tardive dyskinesia. I'll go with G24.

CODE: G24
